newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Crossed wires over Mir spacewalk plan.
newsitem.headline: Crossed wires over Mir spacewalk plan.

text.p: A top Russian space official on Wednesday said NASA had asked Moscow to include an American in an upcoming spacewalk to inspect the damaged Mir space station, contradicting NASA, which said the request was a Russian idea.

The confusion over who wanted British-American astronaut Michael Foale to participate in the important September 3 spacewalk came on the eve of the departure of his two old crewmates, Vasily Tsibliyev and Alexander Lazutkin, due back on Earth on Thursday afternoon.
"It wasn't our request, it was the request of the Americans," said Valery Ryumin, a veteran cosmonaut who heads Russia's cooperation with the U.S. space agency NASA.
"They want to get experience; we responded positively," he told Reuters. "It will probably take place although it has not been decided conclusively."

Last week Mir Flight Director Vladimir Solovyov told reporters Foale would participate in the spacewalk, which will examine a puncture in the Spektr module caused by a collision with Mir's resupply ship on June 25.
Observations made during that spacewalk would help engineers on the ground plan subsequent repairs in which Foale is not expected to participate.

"All of us who were there were as surprised as everyone else was the night Solovyov said Mike Foale would be doing one of the EVAs," said NASA's top official in Russia, Doug Englund, referring to spacewalks. "Clearly a decision had not been made."
At a news conference on Tuesday, Ryumin's U.S. counterpart, Frank Culbertson, said NASA was still considering the request from the Russian space authorities.
"We need to answer some of the concerns we have on safety and make sure we understand truly what the task would be," he said. "That's going to take another day or two probably."
Culbertson said Foale's participation in the spacewalk could provide engineers with a first-hand account of the damage after he returns to Earth aboard the shuttle in early October.

The spacewalkers will also look for other signs of damage on the station's exterior. Russian space officials now believe the out of control cargo craft may have scraped the station's main compartment before ploughing into the Spektr science module.
Asked why NASA would want Foale to do the spacewalk, Ryumin said it would help him gain experience for the future international space station.
"I think he'll probably work on Alpha in the future, so it's probably useful training," he said.

Russian space officials last month had asked NASA if Foale would participate in another risky repair to restore energy from Spektr, but withdrew the idea after they decided a fresh Russian crew that arrived last week should do the work.
